notes: Each case is one user prompt plus the audience the skill is expected to resolve,
and the assertions a graded answer must satisfy. 'audience' must appear verbatim
as a row label in the skill's audience tables -- run_evals.py --check enforces that,
so a case can never test an audience the skill does not define.
expect_trigger=false marks a control case: the prompt contains the word 'explain'
but is NOT an audience request, so the trigger phrases must NOT fire on it.

cases.name: queue-age5
cases.prompt: Explain like I am five what a message queue is
assertions: Contains no technical jargon at all (no 'broker', 'consumer', 'enqueue', 'throughput')
Uses a concrete physical analogy a small child has touched, not an abstract one
Conveys waiting in order -- first in is first served
Warm and delighted in tone, never a definition read aloud

cases.name: rate-limit-manager
cases.prompt: Explain this rate limiting to my manager
assertions: Leads with user or business impact, not with mechanism
Names a cost, a timeline, or a risk in concrete terms
Ends on a decision that is the manager's to make
Does not walk through implementation detail unless asked

cases.name: recursion-age15
cases.prompt: Break this recursion down for a 15 year old
assertions: Correctly conveys that a function calls itself
Mentions a base case or stopping condition
Analogy comes from phones, games, or social apps rather than office work
Casual register without performed teen slang

cases.name: cache-invalidation-default
cases.prompt: Dumb it down: why does cache invalidation keep going wrong
assertions: Defaults to the simplest audience because the phrasing asks for the plainest possible framing and names nobody
Explains staleness -- something kept after it stopped being true
Zero jargon; no 'TTL', 'eviction', or 'coherence'
Does not ask the user which audience to use, because the phrasing already answered that

cases.name: migration-parent
cases.prompt: Explain this database migration to my mom
assertions: Respectful throughout, with no trace of talking down
Analogy drawn from home life or technology she already uses
Conveys that the data moved shape without naming schema mechanics
Warm, conversational register rather than a lecture

cases.name: load-429-designer
cases.prompt: Simplify this for a designer: the API returns 429 under load
assertions: Frames the failure as what the user perceives, not as an HTTP status
Says something about the interaction or flow that breaks
Suggests or implies a design response, such as feedback or a retry state
Avoids backend implementation detail

cases.name: eventual-consistency-graduate
cases.prompt: Explain eventual consistency in plain english for a graduate seminar
assertions: Uses correct terminology rather than avoiding it
Engages a trade-off, a bound, or an edge case instead of only defining the term
Assumes distributed-systems foundations already held
Stays precise -- no analogy that misstates the guarantee

cases.name: merge-conflict-age5
cases.prompt: Explain like I am 5 how git merge conflicts happen
assertions: Conveys two people changing the same thing at once
No version-control vocabulary at all
Analogy uses objects or people a child knows
Short, playful, and encouraging

cases.name: incident-support
cases.prompt: Break this incident down for our support team
assertions: Describes the observable symptom a user would report first
Says how to recognise or confirm the case
States what support should actually do or say
Does not require reading code to be actionable

cases.name: slip-director
cases.prompt: Explain it to my director why the migration slipped two weeks
assertions: Frames the slip against strategy or resource allocation, not task mechanics
Honest about the cause without burying it in detail
States the consequence for the plan going forward
Ends on what is being asked of or decided by the director

cases.name: control-ci-question
cases.prompt: Can you explain for a second why the CI job failed
assertions: Answers the CI question directly
Does not pitch the answer at a child or any other audience level

cases.name: retry-flow-like-a-manager
cases.prompt: explain it to me like a manager: how the retry backoff works
assertions: Leads with what the retry behaviour costs or risks, not with the algorithm
Frames it as a decision or an expectation a manager can hold
Draws a diagram only if it shows the sequence, and does not draw an architecture diagram
Avoids implementation vocabulary like 'jitter' or 'exponential' without a plain gloss

cases.name: lifecycle-diagram-engineer
cases.prompt: Explain this session lifecycle to my teammate, an engineer
assertions: Uses a diagram, because a lifecycle is a sequence of states
The diagram is a mermaid or excalidraw fence rather than ASCII art
The prose carries what the diagram cannot, instead of restating the boxes
Uses real terminology without apologising for it

cases.name: slow-query-middle-school
cases.prompt: explain like im in middle school why this query is slow
assertions: Introduces any technical term together with its definition rather than assuming it
Walks the reason step by step instead of stating a conclusion
Uses a concrete example of the work the database is doing
Does not drop to Age-5 register -- the reader can follow cause and effect

cases.name: control-commit-diff
cases.prompt: Explain the difference between these two commits
assertions: Compares the commits directly
Does not introduce an audience calibration the user never asked for

cases.name: control-explain-it-to-me
cases.prompt: Can you explain it to me
assertions: Explains the thing under discussion directly
Does not pitch the answer at a child or ask which audience to use

cases.name: control-break-this-down
assertions: Breaks the subject down at the level the conversation is already using
Does not pitch the answer at a named audience
